name: Savagnin (Jura)

lines.s10: Savagnin is the Jura's own white, sharp and nutty, and under a veil of yeast it becomes vin jaune, all walnut and curry.
lines.s20: Savagnin grows in the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland, and it keeps a fierce acidity. Kept topped up in cask it is lemon and green apple, and left for years under a veil of yeast it becomes vin jaune, tasting of walnut and curry.
lines.s45: Savagnin is the white they leave alone in the cask for years. Its home is the Jura, the hills between Burgundy and Switzerland. From a cask kept full it tastes of lemon, green apple and quince, bone dry and sharp. Left unfilled, the cask grows a veil of yeast over the wine, and after six years it is vin jaune. That wine is golden and still dry, with walnut, curry and a salty tang. Unlike Sherry, it is never strengthened with spirit. Serve it with Comté cheese, morels or chicken in cream. Its squat bottle, the clavelin, holds what is said to be left of a litre.
lines.sale: Savagnin, as vin jaune, tastes like no other white: bone dry, with walnut, curry and a long, salty finish. I would pour a small glass with the turtle soup, where it does the work of the splash of Sherry, or with Comté at the end.

glass.lead: Lemon, green apple and quince with piercing acidity when topped up; under the veil, walnut, curry and bruised apple with a salty tang.

ladder.where: The Jura's grey marl slopes, topped up or under the veil
Switzerland's Valais, as Heida, in a sunny, dry mountain valley

glass.structure: Bone dry and unfortified. Acidity high, alcohol medium plus, body medium to full; fresh when topped up, broader and more savoury under the veil.

home.home: The Jura, in eastern France, on cool grey marl slopes between Burgundy and Switzerland, where it ripens late and keeps high acidity. Topped up in cask, ouillé, it is fresh and lemony. Left untopped under a veil of yeast it turns nutty and salty, and after more than six years it is vin jaune, never fortified.
home.abroad: Switzerland's Valais grows it high in the Alps as Heida or Païen, a dry, firm white. In Australia, vines planted as Albariño proved in 2009 to be Savagnin, and the wine is now sold under its own name.

service.temp: Vin jaune at 57 to 61 degrees Fahrenheit, 14 to 16 degrees Celsius; a topped up Savagnin cooler.
service.glass: A white wine glass with a generous bowl; pour vin jaune small, for it goes a long way.
service.decant: No need, but open vin jaune a few hours ahead so the scent can unfold.
service.age: Vin jaune is sold in its seventh year and keeps for decades; a topped up Savagnin is poured younger.

with.why: a nutty cheese beside a nutty wine, from the same hills
the Jura's own dish, often cooked with the wine
it does the work of the Sherry in the bowl
sharp acidity cuts through the cream
salt and nuts echo the tang of the veil

labels.means: Savagnin aged under a veil of yeast, untopped, for at least sixty months; sold after six years and three months.
An appellation, not a château: it makes vin jaune and nothing else.
Topped up in cask, so no veil forms: fresh, with lemon and green apple.
Under the veil: aged untopped beneath a film of yeast, nutty and salty.
The squat 62 centilitre bottle kept by law for vin jaune.

guest.q: Is Savagnin the same as Sauvignon Blanc?
guest.a: No, though the names sound alike. Savagnin is the Jura's own grape, from the Traminer family and kin to Gewürztraminer. It is sharper and nuttier, with none of Sauvignon Blanc's cut grass.

guest.q: This smells like Sherry. Has it gone off?
guest.a: No, it is meant to. Vin jaune ages for years under a veil of yeast, as Fino Sherry does, and that gives walnut and curry. Unlike Sherry it is never fortified.

guest.q: I do not care for the nutty style. Is there another Savagnin?
guest.a: Yes. Ask for one marked ouillé. The cask is kept topped up, so no veil forms, and the wine stays fresh: lemon, green apple and a chalky edge.

guest.q: Why is the bottle so small and squat?
guest.a: It is the clavelin, 62 centilitres, kept by law for vin jaune. That is said to be what remains of a litre after more than six years in cask.

compare.tell: Palomino, as Fino Sherry, also ages under a veil of yeast, but it is fortified, lighter and softer in acidity; Savagnin as vin jaune is sharper, with walnut and curry.
Jura Chardonnay, sometimes aged under the veil too, is rounder and less pungent; Savagnin has the sharper acidity and the stronger walnut and curry.
Chenin Blanc aged in air shows bruised apple and honey but none of the curry and fenugreek; Savagnin under the veil has both, with a salty tang.

cards.front: Vin jaune: which grape, how long under the veil, and which bottle?
cards.back: Savagnin alone. At least sixty months untopped under a veil of yeast, sold no sooner than six years and three months after harvest, in the 62 centilitre clavelin. It is never fortified.

cards.front: Savagnin ouillé and sous voile: what differs in the cask and the glass?
cards.back: Ouillé is topped up, so no veil forms: fresh, with lemon and green apple. Sous voile is left untopped under a film of yeast: walnut, curry and a salty tang.

cards.front: Savagnin is no kin of Sauvignon Blanc. Whose kin is it?
cards.back: The Traminer family: it is kin to Gewürztraminer. In the Swiss Valais the same grape is called Heida or Païen.

questions.q: A blind white is deep gold and bone dry, at the strength of a table wine: walnut, curry, bruised apple and a salty tang, with searing acidity. Which wine is it most likely to be?
questions.exp: Walnut and curry from a veil of yeast, with searing acidity and no added spirit, is vin jaune. Fino is fortified, paler and softer in acidity, and shows no curry note.

questions.q: A guest who likes Fino Sherry asks how the vin jaune on the list differs from it in the cellar. Which answer is right?
opts: Vin jaune is aged with no veil of yeast
Vin jaune is sweetened before bottling
Vin jaune is made from dried grapes
questions.exp: Both age under a film of yeast, but vin jaune forms its veil at table wine strength and takes no spirit. Dried grapes make vin de paille, the Jura's sweet wine, not vin jaune.

questions.q: A guest asks why the bottle of Château-Chalon you have brought is squat and holds 62 centilitres, not 75. What do you tell her?
opts: It is the clavelin, kept by law for vin jaune
It is a half bottle, used for sweet wine
It is an old Burgundy measure for village wine
It is the Jura's bottle for sparkling wine
questions.exp: Vin jaune must be sold in the clavelin of 62 centilitres, said to be what remains of a litre after its years in cask. A half bottle holds 37.5 centilitres.

report: Mode home, as the plan fixes it: the Jura, with the Valais and Australia abroad. The name is the roster's own, Savagnin (Jura).

The say line follows the Jura record's respelling, sah-vah-NYAN. The Codex also holds sah-vahn-YAN in the sous voile technique record; the two differ only in where the syllable breaks, and an integrator may wish to make them one.

No Codex record is contradicted. The profile, the dials, the Jura region record and the service reference supplied the fruit, walnut, curry, fenugreek and the salty tang, ouillé and sous voile, the sixty months and the six years and three months, the clavelin and what it is said to hold, Château-Chalon, the Traminer family, the late ripening on grey marl and the table for Comté, morels, chicken in cream and a soup finished with Sherry.

The opening line says the wine is left alone in the cask for years, and the forty-five second line says after six years it is vin jaune: the rule is at least sixty months untopped under the veil and release no sooner than six years and three months after harvest, which the label and the first card state exactly.

Service temperature: the service reference has no row for vin jaune. The Jura's own wine body gives 14 to 16 degrees Celsius, just under room temperature, with the bottle opened a few hours ahead, which agrees with the region record (cool rather than cold, opened ahead). Other guides read through search say 16 to 18.

Abroad: Heida and Païen in the Valais stand on the Valais wine body's page; the Australian vines planted as Albariño and shown by DNA in 2009 to be Savagnin stand on trade reports of that year. Whether Savagnin and Traminer are one variety or a family of close clones is put both ways in the references, so the entry says the Traminer family, as the Codex does.

The moderate rung of the ladder (the Valais: ripe pear, honey, hazelnut) is a taster's reading of the Valais body's own words, which are nuts, honey and exotic and dried fruit without naming the fruit. Hazelnut and toasted almond beside walnut, candied lemon peel and crushed chalk are likewise a taster's reading; the reviewed profile names walnut, lemon and a chalky tension.
The sale says vin jaune tastes like no other white, after the reviewed profile's own tell (nothing else tastes like it); a reader who hears a superlative in it may soften it.

The plan's neighbours include Gewürztraminer; the entry compares Chenin Blanc in its place, since the reviewed profile's confuse line names oxidised Chenin Blanc, and keeps the kinship with Gewürztraminer in a guest answer and a card.
Turtle soup is the one dish from the Creole table: the Codex's Jura record already sends vin jaune to a soup finished with Sherry.
The sources were read through search results; this session could not open the hosts directly.
